name: Anglosphere
scope: The Anglosphere as a political project, as its proponents and the scholars of it state it: the view that the English-speaking, common-law nations (core: the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand; wider: Ireland, English-speaking South Africa, the Caribbean, India and others) share values and institutions (individualism, rule of law, honoring covenants, freedom, representative government) and should draw closer in loose alliance, free trade, free movement and security ties rather than a state, in preference to the European Union or UN-style internationalism. It is Robert Conquest's 'grand Association' of English-speaking nations (s2, s3, s7), James C. Bennett's 'network commonwealth' (s1, s2), and Andrew Roberts's defence of the English-speaking peoples (s3, s4), in the line of Victorian 'Greater Britain' and Churchill's English-speaking peoples (s2, s5, s6). Mycock and Wellings and Pearce describe it the same way, as a transnational orientation for post-Brexit Britain (s5, s6). The strand is the political idea, not the group of countries itself, nor the English language, nor English-speaking world as a linguistic category (Merriam-Webster's definition, s8, is only the dictionary sense). Critics (Ignatieff, Kenny and Pearce, Cohen) are used only to show it is an idea, not for what it holds. Excluded: the Wikipedia-listed countries as such, the 'Anglo-Saxon economic model' as an economics term, and the two downloaded books (a gender-studies volume on Anglophone literature and a history of African labor in the Anglo-American world), which do not define the idea.
summary: The Anglosphere idea holds that the English-speaking common-law nations share a political and cultural inheritance of individual liberty, rule of law and representative government, and that they should cooperate more closely with one another, through security alliances, free trade and easier movement, as a loose network rather than a superstate. Its proponents present it as an alternative to deeper European integration and to UN-style internationalism, and its critics call it a nostalgic or imperial fantasy.

notes: Themes searched: world (UN, EU, NATO, alliances, trade, empire, democracy promotion), government (law, institutions), society and culture (race, language, immigration, nation), economy (trade). Conquest's chapter on the Association and Bennett's thesis (via Windschuttle's review) are the main evidence; Bennett's thesis rests on Windschuttle's review (see notFound for his book). Churchill's History of the English-Speaking Peoples and Conquest's Russia/Soviet books were searched and left uncited: the History is a narrative of the English-speaking peoples with no programme for what the Anglosphere should hold, and the Soviet books are about another subject. The two books found by title (gender-studies and African-labor scholarship) do not define the idea. Proponents differ on how far the union should go: Conquest sketches an Association with joint institutions, Bennett a network that is explicitly not a state; most statements on economics and society are left null because the sources are silent.
